cards.title: AI finds zero-auth bug in gym booking API

panels.head: Anyone could cancel anyone else's gym reservation — no login required
panels.sub: An AI-assisted security researcher found a booking API with no authorisation checks on cancellation endpoints.

panels.head: The target: an Australian gym chain's waitlist system
panels.sub: Waitlists imply a queue — position matters. An unauthenticated cancel call meant you could silently bump yourself up by removing whoever was ahead of you.

panels.head: Researcher confirmed the exploit live: #4 became #3 in real time
panels.sub: The cancellation request was sent against the account of the person holding position #1 on the waitlist — it succeeded without any credential or token belonging to that user.

panels.head: Vibe-coded apps ship features; they often skip auth on state-mutating calls
panels.sub: When LLMs scaffold CRUD logic quickly, authorisation on destructive actions (delete, cancel, revoke) is the class of check most likely to be omitted or assumed to be handled elsewhere.

panels.head: Audit every state-mutating endpoint for caller identity checks — not just input validation
panels.sub: If you ship AI-generated API code, add a review pass specifically for: does this endpoint verify the caller *owns* the resource they're modifying? No amount of rate-limiting fixes a missing ownership check.

cards.title: Docker launches isolated sandboxes for AI agents

panels.head: Agents that can run code are only useful if you can contain them
panels.sub: Letting an AI agent execute arbitrary code against your real filesystem or network is an obvious disaster. Most teams bolt on ad-hoc restrictions and hope for the best.

panels.head: Disposable, API-driven containers spun up per agent task
panels.sub: Docker Sandboxes provision a fresh, fully isolated environment for each agent session — no persistent state, no shared filesystem, killed on completion. Think of it as a per-call VM with container startup speed.

panels.head: Agent requests a sandbox, runs code, environment is destroyed
panels.sub: The sandbox exposes a controlled API surface so the agent can execute commands and read results without touching host resources. Isolation is enforced at the container boundary, not by prompt instruction.

panels.head: Code-execution is the highest-risk tool any agent can hold
panels.sub: With frameworks like LangChain, CrewAI, and Claude tool-use making code execution a default capability, the gap between 'agent can run code' and 'agent can run code safely' has become a shipping blocker for regulated environments.

panels.head: Hard isolation lets you give agents more power without more risk
panels.sub: For PMs shipping agentic workflows in regulated settings — medical imaging pipelines, financial data processing — Docker Sandboxes offers an auditable execution boundary that compliance teams can actually reason about. Worth evaluating before rolling your own chroot/seccomp stack.

cards.title: Long March 7A Fails at T+90s, Payload Lost

panels.head: A Long March 7A rocket exploded less than 90 seconds after liftoff
panels.sub: Amateur video footage captured the explosion, which occurred early in the ascent phase — a window typically associated with first-stage or ignition anomalies.

panels.head: LM-7A is a mid-to-heavy lift workhorse targeting GTO missions
panels.sub: The Long March 7A variant adds a third stage to the base LM-7 to reach geostationary transfer orbit. It had logged several successful flights since its 2021 debut.

panels.head: China has not disclosed what was on board
panels.sub: The payload identity remains undeclared — a common practice for Chinese missions that carry classified government or military satellites.

panels.head: A T+90s failure points to early propulsion, not upper-stage issues
panels.sub: Failures in this flight window usually trigger fleet-wide stand-downs for investigation. Any other LM-7 or LM-7A missions in the manifest could face delays while the root cause is determined.

panels.head: How China handles transparency here signals program maturity
panels.sub: CASC's previous anomaly disclosures have been sparse. The speed and detail of any official statement will indicate how much pressure commercial and government customers are applying for accountability.

cards.title: Mine Reddit for real problems, not app ideas

panels.head: Aspiring founders drown in ideas, not problems
panels.sub: Most 'app idea' lists skip the hard part: proving anyone actually suffers from the problem often enough to pay for a fix. The insight-to-validation gap kills more startups than bad code.

panels.head: Solo founders, indie hackers, product researchers — weekly
panels.sub: Anyone doing customer discovery manually trawls forums, Reddit, and review sites for repeated complaints. It takes hours per vertical and the signal is buried in noise.

panels.head: A 'painfinder' that clusters recurring complaints, not ideas
panels.sub: Scrape public forums, group semantically similar complaints, then surface each cluster with frequency count, emotional intensity, and the workarounds people are already using — raw evidence, not AI-generated ideas.

panels.head: Exploding Topics, SparkToro, and manual Notion boards all fall short
panels.sub: Trend tools track rising search interest, not expressed pain. SparkToro shows audience behaviour, not frustration. Most founders still do this manually, which signals no tool has nailed the job-to-be-done yet.

panels.head: Run the concept as a weekly newsletter before writing a line of code
panels.sub: Manually curate 5 recurring complaints per week from one subreddit (e.g. r/smallbusiness), publish them with frequency data and workaround patterns. If 200 people subscribe in a month, the demand signal is real enough to automate.

panels.head: GitHub Models is gone — no warning, no blog post
panels.sub: Developers discovered the shutdown when GitHub Actions pipelines started failing with a 'scheduled retirement brownout' message that was already out of date.

panels.head: A free, unified LLM API baked into GitHub's own auth
panels.sub: GitHub Models let Actions workflows call multiple LLM providers using the GITHUB_TOKEN already in the environment — no separate API key, no billing setup.

panels.head: Coding agents killed the economics
panels.sub: GitHub never gave an official reason, but the pattern is familiar: agentic coding workflows consume tokens at a rate that makes free or subsidised access unsustainable fast.

panels.head: Drop in a real API key with a spending cap
panels.sub: Simon Willison replaced GitHub Models with an OpenAI key (GPT-5.6 Luna) protected by a monthly spending limit — a two-minute swap for most workflows using the simonw/llm library.

panels.head: Free AI infrastructure in dev tooling is a fragile dependency
panels.sub: If your CI pipelines rely on vendor-subsidised LLM tiers, build in a spending-capped fallback key now — don't wait for a brownout to find out.

cards.title: One inbox for Claude, GPT, and Grok

panels.head: Power users juggle 3+ AI tabs — every day
panels.sub: Knowledge workers who subscribe to Claude Pro, ChatGPT Plus, and Grok Premium still manually decide which tab to open for each task. That decision costs time and often ends in a wrong first pick.

panels.head: The multi-subscription crowd is real and growing
panels.sub: Anyone paying for more than one frontier model likely has a routing problem — analysts, PMs, researchers, and developers who've learned each model has different strengths across coding, reasoning, and long-context tasks.

panels.head: Bring your own keys, skip the tab-switching
panels.sub: A lightweight router sits in front of your existing API subscriptions: classify the query, pick the best-fit model, optionally fan out to two models in parallel for comparison. No new AI, just better plumbing on top of models you're already paying for.

panels.head: Chatbot aggregators exist but don't route — they just list
panels.sub: Tools like Nat.dev or OpenRouter let you switch models manually. They expose the complexity rather than abstracting it. The routing and deliberation layer — deciding for you, then surfacing disagreements — is still missing.

panels.head: Test before building
panels.sub: Post a one-question survey to AI-power-user communities: 'How many frontier model subscriptions do you pay for, and do you have a decision rule for which to use?' If most respondents say 2+ subs and 'I just guess,' the pain is real. Then build a landing page with a waitlist before writing a line of code.

cards.title: SQLite revision history: 20 MB → 80 KB with zstd

panels.head: Storing every edit of a 20 KB doc costs 20 KB per save
panels.sub: Naive revision history — one row per version — balloons fast. A document edited 1,000 times generates ~20 MB of near-identical text with no deduplication.

panels.head: Pack all versions into one compressed JSON blob
panels.sub: Simon Willison's dog-walk insight: store every prior version as a JSON array of strings, then compress the whole thing with zstd. Adjacent versions are almost identical, so compression ratios are extreme.

panels.head: 1,000 revisions: 20.4 MB raw → 80.3 KB compressed
panels.sub: A GPT-5.6 Sol Pro session (38 minutes, one text prompt) built working Python prototypes. The 254× compression ratio holds because zstd exploits repeated strings across the full array in one pass.

panels.head: Chunk rows at 128 revisions or 3 MB to keep writes fast
panels.sub: Recompressing a single growing blob on every edit gets expensive. The model suggested splitting history into multiple rows with a size cap — each append only touches the latest chunk.

panels.head: A voice brainstorm + one prompt → shippable SQLite schema
panels.sub: For any app storing versioned text (notes, config files, form drafts), this pattern gives near-free history with zero external store. The workflow — narrate the idea aloud, then prompt for prototypes — is itself worth stealing.

cards.title: No e-ink UI toolkit exists. Someone should build one.

panels.head: E-ink phones are real. Web UIs for them are a disaster.
panels.sub: A developer switches to a Bigme Hibreak Pro to escape the attention economy — then finds that every browser-based UI (HN, LLM chat, social feeds) is actively hostile to e-ink: ghosting, constant redraws, streaming text, dark gradients.

panels.head: E-ink smartphone owners are a small but growing niche with zero tailored tooling.
panels.sub: Onyx Boox, Hisense, Bigme, and others sell Android e-ink phones. Buyers are deliberate, privacy-minded, and technically capable — exactly the people who will pay for and contribute to a well-designed solution.

panels.head: Three unsolved design problems: refresh control, pagination, and greyscale-only layout.
panels.sub: Streaming LLM output must be chunked and painted in bursts. Scrolling causes ghosting, so pagination must replace it cleanly. Typography and layout must carry the full UI — no colour, no shadows, no gradients. No existing CSS framework treats any of these as first-class concerns.

panels.head: Native e-ink apps exist; a reusable web layer does not.
panels.sub: KOReader handles e-reader content well, but it's a closed, document-centric app. Generic React/Tailwind sites ignore e-ink constraints entirely. There is no open CSS framework or component library built around refresh budgets and greyscale contrast.

panels.head: Hypothesis, not a business — test it cheap before building it broad.
panels.sub: Search GitHub and the Onyx/Boox forums for e-ink CSS or UI conventions threads. If the same three questions keep appearing with no accepted answers, that's your signal. A single open-source component library with a live demo on an e-ink device would pull contributors fast.
